newsitem.title: USA: Vote to scrap U.S. drug certification plan.
newsitem.headline: Vote to scrap U.S. drug certification plan.

text.p: A bill to scrap the process under which the U.S. president certifies the performance of foreign countries in fighting drug smuggling is headed for debate in the House of Representatives.

The bill, a wide-ranging foreign affairs and foreign aid measure approved late on Tuesday, includes a provision that would replace the certification system with one under which imposition of sanctions against countries failing to act against smuggling would be left up to the president.
The current system has been criticised as a blunt instrument that does nothing to intensify the fight against drugs and only serves to offend other countries.
The House International Relations Committee's approved the bill while President Bill Clinton was on a visit to Mexico.

Clinton certified Mexico as an anti-narcotics ally in February, but the House voted to overturn the certification, angering Mexico. The Senate, after intensive administration lobbying, approved a mild measure that left certification intact. Colombia was "decertified" for a second year.

Under the new legislation, proposed by Representative Lee Hamilton, an Indiana Democrat, the president would have discretionary authority to cut aid to major drug producing, drug transiting or money laundering countries when counter-narcotics goals would be served.
It eliminates the practice of grading countries annually on their performance.
Hamilton said he looked forward to working with committee chairman Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, and the Clinton administration on improving the legislation.
